summary: GameGo expands about 67k scraped game descriptions into long LLM-written Product Requirements Documents (median 9,136 tokens), compresses each into a roughly 235-token task query, and has an undisclosed ('confidential') frontier teacher build each game as a React app in a sandbox. The resulting 55,060 trajectories are used to fine-tune Qwen 27B models (GameGoCoder). On 124 held-out game tasks, six blinded human raters preferred games built from the compressed query over the full PRD (0.857) and over a direct rewrite of the seed (0.866), and the full PRD over the direct query (0.690). The fine-tuned models beat their bases (+18 points for Qwen3.5-27B, +2 to +4 for Qwen3.8-27B) but stay below Claude Opus 5 on every benchmark.

claims.claim: GameGoCoder outperforms matched base models across game-development benchmarks
claims.evidence: Table 1 and Table 5: Qwen3.5-27B 34.00 -> 51.85 on GameGoBench and 46.31 -> 57.34 on ArtifactsBench-G; Qwen3.8-27B 52.53 -> 55.29, 59.87 -> 61.94 and 77.07 -> 80.68. Gains persist under three LLM verifiers and blinded human preference, but each model makes one rollout per query and no intervals are given.

claims.claim: GameGoCoder is comparable to frontier models and achieves state-of-the-art results across public benchmarks and GameGoBench
claims.evidence: Table 1: Claude Opus 5 leads every Overall column (61.84 vs 55.29 on GameGoBench; 72.76 vs 61.94 on ArtifactsBench-G); GameGoCoder 3.8 trails 5 of 6 frontier models on ArtifactsBench-G. 'Comparable' holds only against the weaker frontier models; 'state-of-the-art' (contribution bullet) is contradicted by the table.

claims.claim: Compressed task-specific queries yield better games than full PRDs (85.7% preference) and direct queries (86.6%)
claims.evidence: Table 2 and App F: 124 pairs per comparison, six blinded reviewers, raw agreement 81.7% (no chance-corrected statistic); one undisclosed teacher, one rollout per condition, no intervals; pooled reviewer judgments, so the effective sample is 124 tasks. Quality is judged against the original seed, not the PRD.
claims.location: Section 5.4.1, Table 2, App D, App F

claims.claim: Compression preserves core gameplay constraints with a median 3.79x relation-density gain
claims.evidence: App G: an AI-assisted audit of 927 sampled PRD clauses finds 12.1% complete, 62.2% partial and 25.7% absent in the query; 56 of 124 tasks have zero complete clauses. The density gain exceeds 1 mainly because of 44x compression.

claims.claim: All code, datasets and models will be made publicly available
claims.evidence: App H: prompt specifications are to be released 'upon acceptance' and 'This release does not include GameGoData trajectories'; the teacher model is described as confidential (App D).

patterns.note: Spec-first expansion helps but handing the agent the whole spec hurts. A full PRD beat a direct seed rewrite (0.690), yet a ~235-token query distilled from the PRD beat both the 9,136-token PRD (0.857) and the direct query (0.866), with the same teacher, scaffold and budget (Table 2). One teacher and one rollout per condition, in a creative domain judged against the seed.

A structured PRD (state transitions, controls, failure conditions, asset contracts) beats an unstructured direct query (0.690), but the compressed query, which leaves 25.7% of sampled clauses out entirely and 62.2% partially expressed, wins by more (Table 2, App G).
Underspecified requests are resolved by LLM-invented PRD detail rather than by asking the user; no comparison with clarifying questions.
Planning calls retrieve genre and rendering guidance plus small 'expert cards' (combat, level flow, assets) as domain context (App C.3); not ablated.

A Claude Sonnet 4.6 agent verifier plays and scores each game; model rankings are stable across three verifier families (Spearman 0.964/0.976, Table 5) and broadly match blinded human preference, but no per-item human-verifier agreement is reported.

SFT on teacher trajectories beats the untuned base, but there is no data-matched control (for example SFT on direct-query trajectories) because of cost (App D); the gain on the stronger backbone is 2-4 points with one rollout.

methodology.sample: 67,564 queries -> 55,060 trajectories; GameGoBench 124 held-out tasks (47 2D, 22 2.5D, 55 3D); ArtifactsBench-G 413 and Cookie-Bench-G 156 tasks; human study of 124 pairs x 6 reviewers per comparison.
methodology.baselines: Matched base Qwen3.5-27B and Qwen3.8-27B; six frontier models in the same Code Arena scaffold; for task representations, a direct seed rewrite (DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision-Exp) and the full PRD.
methodology.models: Undisclosed 'confidential' teacher; students Qwen3.5-27B and Qwen3.8-27B (full SFT) and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B base MoE; verifiers Claude Sonnet 4.6, DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision-Exp and Qwen3.8-Max.
methodology.variance: One rollout per query, one training seed; only cross-verifier variance reported; no intervals on human preferences.
methodology.ablations: Task representation (direct vs full PRD vs compressed) at artifact level; MoE base-model training epochs; no SFT-level ablation of representation.
methodology.contamination_controls: Benchmark seeds separated before pipeline development, but benchmark tasks pass through the same PRD and compression pipeline, so GameGoBench is in-distribution for GameGoCoder.

standards.peer_review: arXiv preprint; ICLR ethics statement suggests a submission
standards.artifacts: GitHub link given; prompts promised upon acceptance; trajectories excluded from release (App H) despite the abstract; teacher undisclosed

biases.detail: GameGoBench queries come from the same PRD/compression pipeline as the training data, which favours GameGoCoder over models it is compared with.
Authors' benchmark, authors' pipeline and authors' model.
Benchmark scores come from an LLM agent verifier validated only by cross-verifier rank agreement.
Single rollout per query and condition; no intervals.
'State-of-the-art' and 'comparable to frontier models' while Claude Opus 5 leads every column.
Confidential teacher; trajectories not released; prompts only upon acceptance.
Relation density counts only complete clauses per token, so 44x compression yields a 'gain' even when 87.9% of clauses are partial or absent.

coi.affiliations: Baidu Inc.; Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: Authors' own GameGoCoder (on Qwen bases) and their own benchmark; no Baidu commercial model evaluated
coi.detail: Vendor-affiliated authors grade their own model on their own benchmark with an undisclosed teacher and no independent replication; the model is not a commercial product and does not top the leaderboard.

verdict_reason: Only the task-representation ablation bears on this knowledge base: a blinded, 124-task, six-rater comparison showing that a short query distilled from a long LLM-written PRD beats both the PRD and the raw request. It is admitted at low weight because the teacher is undisclosed, every condition is one rollout without intervals, the domain rewards creative freedom, and the abstract and contributions overstate frontier parity and artifact release.
applicability: Indirect. In a spec-driven flow an agent could expand a terse ticket into a long LLM-written spec and hand all of it to the coder. Here that lost to a short brief distilled from the spec, and the full spec beat the raw request only 69 to 31. But quality was judged against the original seed, so dropping invented detail cost nothing. In Java ingestion services the detail that matters (field mappings, contract versions, edge cases) is real requirement, not invention, and other papers in this knowledge base find missing implicit requirements to be a leading failure cause. For the pre-spec harness, the lesson is to keep the discovery/spec artifact (long, for humans and traceability) separate from the execution brief given to the coding agent (short), and to check the brief's omissions against the spec rather than drop them silently; GameGo's own audit found 25.7% of sampled clauses missing. It gives no evidence on clarifying questions, because underspecification was filled by LLM invention.

conflicts_with.detail: SWE-RPG finds missing implicit requirements (interfaces, conventions, data semantics) are the most common failure stage for coding agents and argues for more explicit requirements; GameGo finds a compressed brief that fully keeps only 12.1% of sampled clauses produces better artifacts than the full spec. Different domains and judges (test-verified issue resolution vs seed-referenced game preference).

Expert refinement that spelled out exact constants, defaults and signatures turned failing SWE-Bench Pro tasks into passes; GameGo's compression drops such parameters (clauses labelled partial) and still wins on human preference, because nothing tests those parameters.
